payload.wikitext: {{Short description|Genus of ornithopod dinosaur}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = [[Early Cretaceous]], {{fossilrange|Barremian|Barremian|[[Barremian]]}} | image = Paludohadros proudlovii.png | image_caption = [[Life restoration]] | display_parents = 2 | genus = Paludohadros | parent_authority = Sacamoto et al., [[2026 in archosaur paleontology|2026]] | species = proudlovii | authority = Sacamoto et al., 2026 }} '''''Paludohadros''''' ({{lit|swamp hadrosauroid}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[hadrosauroid]] ornithopod dinosaur known from the [[Early Cretaceous]] ([[Barremian]] age) [[Weald Clay Formation]] of the United Kingdom. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Paludohadros proudlovii''''', known from a partial skull and skeleton, as well as various isolated remains. It is one of several [[iguanodontia]]n dinosaurs known from the [[Weald Basin]], though all others are from older [[Valanginian]] rock layers, including ''[[Barilium]]'', ''[[Hypselospinus]]'', and ''[[Kukufeldia]]''. == Discovery and naming == On July 22, 2001, the British [[Geologists' Association]] conducted a field trip to [[Smokejack Clay Pit]] (now Ewhurst Works) near the village of [[Ockley]] in [[Surrey]], UK. This site, which exposes outcrops of the [[Weald Clay Formation]], is known for yielding the holotype specimen of the [[spinosaurid]] theropod ''[[Baryonyx walkeri]]'' in 1983. During the 2001 excursion, Geoff Toye discovered a partial iguanodontian skull and skeleton in the same rock layer that produced the ''Baryonyx'' specimen, albeit around {{convert|100|m|ft}} west. The site was excavated throughout the next two weeks with the assistance of the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] (NHMUK), during which several limb bones were recovered, but only three vertebrae, all of which came from the tail. Two ''Baryonyx'' teeth were recovered as well, a possible indication that the iguanodont carcass was [[scavenged]]. An initial report by the Geologists' Association in October, 2001 identified the remains as belonging to a juvenile ''[[Iguanodon]]''. In 2008, a formal publication described the palaeoenvironment of the quarry that yielded this specimen, focused on fossil [[pollen]] and [[ostracod]]s. The iguanodont fossil was ultimately donated to the NHMUK, where it is now permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen NHMUK PV R 16396. It consists of a partial skull (including several bones of the cranium, braincase, palate, and mandible) and various [[postcrania]]l remains, including {{dinogloss|rib}} fragments, the right {{dinogloss|pectoral girdle}}, much of both forelimbs, the right {{dinogloss|ischium}} (a {{dinogloss|pelvis|pelvic bone}}), parts of both hindlimbs, and three {{dinogloss|caudals|caudal (tail) vertebrae}}. In a 2021 review of Smokejacks fossils, these "''Iguanodon''" remains were instead regarded as belonging to the related genus ''[[Mantellisaurus]]''. In 2026, Ricardo J. Sacamoto and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Paludohadros proudlovii'' as a new genus and species of hadrosauroid dinosaur based on these fossil remains, designating NHMUK PV R 16396 as the [[holotype]] specimen. Four {{dinogloss|humeri}} and four {{dinogloss|tibiae}} from Smokejack Pit, described by W. H. E. Rivett in 1953 and 1956, were referred to this species, as was an isolated partial {{dinogloss|surangular}} (part of the mandible) from a different [[Wealden Group|Wealden]] site (which the authors suggested probably originated from the [[Wessex Formation]]) on the [[Isle of Wight]]. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Paludohadros'', combines the [[Latin]] word {{lang|la|[[:wikt:palus#Latin|palūs]]}}, meaning {{gloss|swamp}}, with the [[Greek language|Greek]] {{lang|grc|[[:wikt:ἁδρός|ἁδρός]]}} ({{lang|grc|hadrós}}), a suffix often used in hadrosauroid genus names meaning {{gloss|stout}} or {{gloss|robust}}. This references the swampy environment this taxon would have inhabited during the Cretaceous, as well as the current muddy conditions of the type locality. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''proudlovii'', honors William Proudlove, who managed the Smokejack Pit and died in 2000, shortly before the excavation of the holotype. == Description == The ''P. proudlovii'' holotype individual is estimated to have been about {{convert|5|m|ft}} long. The unfused vertebrae and rugose texture on the limb bones both suggest this individual was not fully mature when it died. The femur is {{cvt|63|cm|in}} long, intermediate between the holotypes of ''[[Mantellisaurus atherfieldensis]]'' ({{cvt|57|cm|in}}) and ''[[Comptonatus chasei]]'' ({{cvt|73.5|cm|in}}), both of represent more mature animals. The femora of mature ''[[Iguanodon bernissartensis]]'' are around {{cvt|104|cm|in}} long, with mature individuals reaching up to around {{cvt|11|m|ft}} in length. It is thus possible that ''Paludohadros'' could have reached comparable sizes when fully grown. This is supported by specimen NHMUK PV R 105a, the referred isolated surangular found on the Isle of Wight, which belongs to a much larger individual than the holotype. The skeleton of ''Paludohadros'' is distinguished from other iguanodontians by several anatomical characters, including the number of ridges on the teeth of the lower jaw, the presence of a well developed dorsally (upward) projecting lateral process of the {{dinogloss|surangular}} bone of the lower jaw, the distal condyle of the {{dinogloss|humerus}} having a ridge that projects proximally (towards the body), the ischium curving posteroventrally (backwards and downwards) and has a well developed boot, and a tibia with bosses (growths) on the proximal end (closest to the knee joint). == Classification == To test the affinities and relationships of ''Paludohadros'', Sacamoto et al. (2026) included it in an updated version of the [[phylogenetic]] matrix of Poole (2022). They recovered it as the [[sister taxon]] to ''[[Istiorachis]]'', another Wealden taxon from the [[Wessex Formation]]. This clade of early-diverging [[hadrosauroid]]s also included ''[[Xuwulong]]'' and ''[[Kukufeldia]]''. gobiensis]]'' |2=[[Hadrosauromorpha]] [[File:Life reconstruction of Parasaurolophus walkeri.png|80px]] }} }} }} }} }} }} }} }} }} }}|label1=[[Styracosterna]]}} == Palaeoecology == [[File:Paludohadros proudlovii (life restoration by Guilherme Gehr).png|thumb|Life restoration of ''Paludohadros'' (foreground) and ''Baryonyx'' (background) in the Weald Clay palaeoenvironment]] ''Paludohadros'' is known from the [[Weald Clay Formation]], a unit of the [[Wealden Group]] that dates to the [[Barremian]] age of the early [[Cretaceous]] period. The Wealden Group is split into two major subunits: the [[Weald Basin]] (to which the Weald Clay belongs) and the [[Wessex Basin]]. Many other [[styracosterna]]n ornithopod dinosaurs are known from the other formations in these units, though ''Paludohadros'' is the first one named from the Weald Clay, as well as the first named based on fossils from Barremian-aged rocks in the Weald Basin. Other Weald Basin iguanodontians, such as ''[[Barilium]]'', ''[[Hypselospinus]]'', and ''[[Kukufeldia]]'', derive from other [[Valanginian]]-aged rocks. Analyses of the outcrops of the Weald Clay at Smokejack Clay Pit indicate that it was deposited in [[marshy]] conditions, the region being a shallow, temporary [[floodplain]]. [[Schizaeaceae|Schizaceous]] ferns and [[tree ferns]] were the predominant [[undergrowth]] components within [[conifer]] forests. Dinosaurs are the best-represented vertebrate fossils in the Weald Clay Formation. In addition to ''Paludohadros'', the [[spinosaurid]] theropod ''[[Baryonyx]]'' is also known from the Smokejack Clay Pit. Other localities have produced the indeterminate [[maniraptora]]n theropod ''[[Wyleyia]]'', the ankylosaur ''[[Horshamosaurus]]'', and the [[dryosaurid]] ornithopod ''[[Valdosaurus]]''. == References == {{Reflist|refs= {{Cite journal |last1=Sacamoto |first1=Ricardo J. |last2=Lockwood |first2=Jeremy A.
